html: The single most striking result in the noise literature is about timing, not dose. Noise during the sleep phase causes the blood pressure rise, the endothelial dysfunction, the oxidative stress and the uncoupling of the synthase; the same noise during the waking phase does much less, and in the redox and endothelial readouts does nothing at all. The transcriptome of the exposed aorta points at two things: the circadian clock, dysregulated across aorta, heart and kidney, and FOXO3, down. This module draws what can be drawn of that. FOXO3 is the hub, and its switch is where it sits: the kinase AKT phosphorylates it, 14-3-3 binds the phosphorylated form and keeps it in the cytoplasm, and only the unphosphorylated factor reaches the nucleus. There it is read at two genes. One is the manganese superoxide dismutase, which is the canonical target and the reason the factor's loss is an antioxidant loss; the brain of a noise-exposed mouse also loses catalase message alongside the factor's own. The other is CLOCK: the factor binds two elements in its promoter, and without the factor the circadian amplitude falls and comes back when CLOCK is put back. That is the one edge that makes the clock changes mechanism rather than a heat map, and it is drawn at CLOCK and not at BMAL1 for a reason worth stating. The noise paper asserts a FOXO3 site on the Bmal1 promoter, but that sentence has no experiment and no citation behind it, and no study of any FOXO at that promoter exists; the CLOCK result does. It was found in liver, so on a vascular map it is an extrapolation, which the statement says. The rest of the loop is drawn as it is known, CLOCK and BMAL1 together reading the period gene, the period-cryptochrome pair carried back into the nucleus to shut the dimer that made them. What is deliberately not drawn is an arrow from noise to any single clock gene. The individual genes come from sequencing with no direction stated and no perturbation, and inventing arrows from a heat map would be the easiest way to make this module look more certain than it is.
